section_summary: This section comprises diverse records relating to American-Japanese educational and cultural relations, dating from 1917 to 1941. It begins with an excerpt from an English-language Nisei periodical covering university football, poetry, and war correspondents, followed by State Department correspondence regarding an editorial on Dean M. Lyle Spencer's appointment to a Tokyo summer college. The majority of the section consists of Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 4898 transmitting the 1917 founding correspondence and biographical materials for the Hepburn Professorship of American Constitution, History and Diplomacy at Tokyo Imperial University, concluding with a cross-reference note on dual-nationality students.

subfiles.about: A published excerpt from an English-language Nisei magazine covering Tokyo collegiate football, poetry, Nisei war correspondents, community movements, and local commercial advertisements.
subfiles.summary: This excerpt from an English-language Nisei periodical opens with a feature article reviewing the 1939 championship race of the Tokyo Intercollegiate Football League among Meiji, Waseda, Keio, Hosei, and Rikkyo universities, offering tactical analysis, rosters, and background on the sport's development in Japan since 1933. It is followed by anonymous student poetry, brief personal news on Japanese Americans traveling or returning home, and an article by Ken Murayama describing the experiences of Nisei war correspondents in China and Europe. The concluding pages contain advertisements for Tokyo businesses catering to English speakers and Japanese Americans, including dressmaking schools, pharmacies, tailoring, cultured pearls, and printing services.
subfiles.title: King Football Returns to Japanese Gridiron [and Other Articles]

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum suggesting a routine acknowledgment of a letter from Joseph J. Early regarding Dean M. Lyle Spencer.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs advises the Division of Cultural Relations on how to acknowledge a letter and editorial submitted by Joseph J. Early. The memorandum recommends a simple statement noting that the material was carefully examined and expressing appreciation for Mr. Early's courtesy. It also states that the Secretary of State does not need to sign the reply personally.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Acknowledgment of Letter from Joseph J. Early

subfiles.about: An internal routing note asking whether a commendatory note should be drafted for the Secretary's signature to Joseph J. Early.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Cultural Relations (RC:HHP) queries the Division of Far Eastern Affairs (FE) concerning an incoming communication from Joseph J. Early. The memorandum asks whether it would be advisable to draft a brief commendatory reply for the signature of Secretary of State Cordell Hull.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Proposed Commendatory Note to Joseph J. Early

subfiles.about: A letter transmitting a newspaper editorial regarding Dean M. Lyle Spencer's teaching appointment in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Joseph J. Early of Brooklyn, New York, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmitting an editorial from the Queens Evening News of Jamaica, New York. The editorial concerns the appointment and upcoming journey of Dean M. Lyle Spencer of Syracuse University to teach at the Oriental Cultural Summer College in Tokyo. Early brings the article to the Secretary's attention as an example of Japanese-American cultural cooperation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph J. Early to Secretary of State Cordell Hull

subfiles.about: An official letter acknowledging receipt of an editorial concerning Dean M. Lyle Spencer's faculty appointment in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Charles A. Thomson, Assistant Chief of the Division of Cultural Relations, replies on behalf of the Department of State to Joseph J. Early's letter of May 4, 1940. He acknowledges the enclosed editorial from the Queens Evening News concerning the appointment of Dean M. Lyle Spencer of Syracuse University to the faculty of the Oriental Cultural Summer College at Tokyo. Thomson states that the editorial was carefully noted and thanks Early for bringing the matter to the Secretary's attention.
subfiles.title: Letter from Charles A. Thomson to Joseph J. Early

subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum briefing Stanley K. Hornbeck on Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 4898 concerning the Hepburn Professorship.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 4898 for Adviser on Political Relations Stanley K. Hornbeck. The memo explains that the Hepburn Professorship at Tokyo Imperial University was established in 1917 through an endowment of 120,000 yen in Japanese Government bonds by A. Barton Hepburn to provide instruction on American institutions, history, and diplomacy. It reports that copies of the original correspondence were collected to complete Embassy records and transmitted for departmental reference, requiring no further action.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Hepburn Professorship at Tokyo Imperial University

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch transmitting historical correspondence and reporting on the status of the Hepburn Professorship at Tokyo Imperial University.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits copies of the 1917 correspondence between A. Barton Hepburn, Baron Eiichi Shibusawa, and Baron Kenjiro Yamagawa regarding the foundation of the Hepburn Professorship of American Constitution, History and Diplomacy. Grew notes that complete records had been lacking in the Embassy files and outlines the terms of the original gift of Japanese loan bonds and cash. He describes the role of the custodial committee, on which the American Ambassador serves ex officio, and notes that the current chair holder, Dr. Yasaka Takagi, delivers well-attended lectures. Grew also transmits a biographical sketch of Dr. James Curtis Hepburn, whose missionary career inspired the endowment.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4898: Transmitting Copies of Certain Letters Exchanged in 1917 Regarding the Hepburn Professorship

subfiles.about: A letter from A. Barton Hepburn detailing the financial provisions and administrative arrangements for endowing the American professorship.
subfiles.summary: A. Barton Hepburn formally addresses Baron Kenjiro Yamagawa, President of Tokyo Imperial University, regarding the endowment of a chair titled 'American Constitution, History and Diplomacy.' Hepburn confirms the purchase of over 115,000 yen in Kogo 5% bonds deposited with the Yokohama Specie Bank and placed at the disposal of Baron Shibusawa and a custodial committee. He agrees that the chair should be filled by a Japanese scholar who will receive three years of preparatory training in America, followed by quadrennial study visits. Hepburn endorses public lectures across Japan to foster mutual understanding between the Japanese and American peoples.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. Barton Hepburn to Baron K. Yamagawa

subfiles.about: A letter conveying Tokyo Imperial University's proposal to adjust the title, scope, and staffing of the proposed American professorship.
subfiles.summary: Baron Kenjiro Yamagawa, President of Tokyo Imperial University, writes to Baron Eiichi Shibusawa outlining the University Council's recommendations regarding A. Barton Hepburn's endowment offer. Yamagawa explains that because the university already maintains chairs in international law, the new chair should focus instead on American history, constitutional law, and diplomacy to better promote mutual understanding. He advocates appointing a Japanese scholar rather than an American to avoid language barriers and salary disparities, proposing that a chosen candidate be sent to the United States for three years of study supported by endowment income.
subfiles.title: Letter from Baron K. Yamagawa to Baron Eiichi Shibusawa

subfiles.about: A comprehensive letter discussing bilateral relations, immigration questions, and Hepburn's original proposal to endow a professorship in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: A. Barton Hepburn writes to Baron Eiichi Shibusawa analyzing the geopolitical and social forces shaping American-Japanese relations during World War I. He argues that Japanese immigrants qualify for American naturalization on equal footing with Europeans, but explains how domestic labor opposition and the subversive wartime sabotage committed by German-Americans have intensified American demands for immigration restriction. To counteract anti-Japanese prejudice and promote mutual comity, Hepburn offers 100,000 yen in Japanese loan bonds to establish a professorship at Tokyo Imperial University. He recalls that his missionary relative, Dr. James Curtis Hepburn, had strongly urged him always to remain a friend to the Japanese people.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. Barton Hepburn to Baron Eiichi Shibusawa

subfiles.about: A letter acknowledging receipt of the endowment funds and confirming initial arrangements for the Hepburn Professorship.
subfiles.summary: Baron Kenjiro Yamagawa writes to A. Barton Hepburn acknowledging receipt into the Tokyo Imperial University Treasury of 120,000 yen in Japanese Imperial Loan Bonds and 3,000 yen in cash delivered via Baron Shibusawa. He details how the income will be expended for the professor's salary, travel, assistants, and library acquisitions, and notes that a young scholar will be selected for three years of preparatory study in the United States. Yamagawa adds that during the interim, distinguished scholars including Dr. Inazo Nitobe and Viscount Kentaro Kaneko will be invited to give lectures, and confirms the composition of the custodial committee.
subfiles.title: Letter from Baron K. Yamagawa to A. Barton Hepburn

subfiles.about: A biographical sketch describing the life and missionary accomplishments of Dr. James Curtis Hepburn in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This document reproduces an excerpt from Joseph Bucklin Bishop's authorized biography of A. Barton Hepburn, detailing the career of Dr. James Curtis Hepburn (1815-1911). It traces Dr. Hepburn's origins in Pennsylvania, education at Princeton, and pioneering service as a medical missionary in Japan starting in 1859. The text highlights his monumental linguistic contributions, including compiling the first Japanese-English dictionary, translating the Bible into Japanese, and establishing medical and religious institutions. It notes how Dr. Hepburn's deep regard for the Japanese people influenced A. Barton Hepburn's philanthropy.
subfiles.title: Biographical Sketch of Dr. James Curtis Hepburn

subfiles.about: A cross-reference note indexing a telegram concerning Japanese governmental concern over dual-nationality Nisei students.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference note references a midnight telegram (#861) sent by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on June 22, 1941, filed under 811.111 Matumoto, Takizo. It summarizes the Japanese Government's embarrassment caused by the influx of uninvited, uninformed, and disappointed second-generation students with dual nationality. The note records the official Japanese position that dual nationals should elect their nationality before traveling to Japan, and states Japan's desire to provide non-Japanese students with education consistent with their foreign status.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note regarding Dual Nationality Students in Japan
